title: To Read a 2,000-Year-Old Library, Scientists Burned Their Own Scrolls First
summary:
When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E., it buried Pompeii — and also a Roman town called Herculaneum, where volcanic ash carbonized more than a thousand papyrus scrolls in a library. Those charred lumps are now the only intact library to survive from the ancient world. The problem? Try to unroll one and it crumbles into black dust. Early attempts in the 1750s were so disastrous that Italian authorities eventually banned the practice.

Douglas Seiler thinks there's a way to read them without opening them — and he tested it by burning his own scrolls on purpose. He ordered papyrus and reed pens from Egypt and traditional lampblack ink from Japan, then paid high school students to write passages from Star Wars, the Bible, and the 1960s show The Outer Limits. Then he carbonized the scrolls and scanned them with X-ray tomography (a 3D X-ray scan, like a hospital CT scan for scrolls).

His hypothesis: if ancient ink contained lead, that metal would absorb X-rays far more strongly than carbonized papyrus. He was right. Even tiny amounts of lead produced a dramatic signal — absorbing up to 25 times more X-rays than the surrounding burned paper. "With lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature," Seiler said. The team also found that a cheap handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner can quickly detect lead ink, letting researchers screen scrolls before committing to detailed scans.

So far, only a few Herculaneum scrolls have been virtually opened, and none were first tested for lead. The collection holds about 1,800 scrolls and fragments across Italy, France, and England. Every scroll physically opened in the past contained writing otherwise lost to history — many works by Philodemus, an Epicurean philosopher who lived about a century before the eruption.

"The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature," said Leah Packard-Grams, a papyrologist who consulted on the project. Next step: a systematic search for lead across the whole collection. If it works, we could read books that have been silent for two thousand years.
why_it_matters: If the lead test works across the whole library, texts that have been silent for two thousand years could be read again — which means lost works of ancient philosophy, science, and storytelling may still be sitting in museum storerooms, waiting for a scanner instead of a hand.

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in southern Italy) erupted in 79 C.E. and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and hot volcanic gas. Herculaneum's library, often called the Villa of the Papyri, is the only large library to survive from the ancient world, and its scrolls were carbonized rather than completely burned away.

Ancient books were written on papyrus, sheets made from reeds that grew along the Nile, and then rolled into scrolls. Philodemus (an Epicurean philosopher who lived about a century before the eruption) is the author of many of the texts recovered from the library so far.

For more than two hundred years, scholars who tried to peel the scrolls open destroyed them, and the pieces that survived still gave historians lost works of Greek philosophy. In recent years a prize contest called the Vesuvius Challenge (funded by technology donors) has pushed teams to read unopened scrolls using extremely bright X-ray scans and machine-learning software, and a few words have been recovered that way.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: technology can recover what was thought lost
perspectives.description: Every scroll that was physically opened in the past contained writing otherwise lost to history, so the upside is enormous — complete works by authors we only know by name. Because a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner can spot lead quickly and cheaply, small teams can screen hundreds of scrolls before spending money on detailed scans. Supporters see this as a turning point where reading no longer requires destroying.

perspectives.perspective: Critical: a self-made test may not match the real thing
perspectives.description: Seiler tested his idea on scrolls he had made and burned himself, with modern ink recipes, so there is no guarantee that the ancient scrolls contain lead at all — ink recipes varied by workshop, region, and century. Burning new papyrus also cannot perfectly reproduce how volcanic heat and gas changed the originals over centuries. A negative result might say more about the experiment than about the scroll.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: a familiar pattern of damage followed by repair
perspectives.description: The story follows a pattern seen in archaeology many times: one generation damages artefacts while trying to save them, and a later generation invents a non-destructive method. The 1750s attempts destroyed scrolls that scholars now wish they had left alone, and the field has since moved from physically unrolling to scanning and even crowdsourced contests that invite outsiders to help decode the images.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: scaling up from a handful to a whole library
perspectives.description: So far only a few Herculaneum scrolls have been virtually opened, and none were first checked for lead ink, so the real test is still ahead. If the systematic survey succeeds, the method could be applied to other charred or fragile documents elsewhere in the world. The open questions are practical: who pays for the scanning time, who gets access to the images, and how quickly can such a large collection be worked through.
